title: Map Meters per Pixel Calculator: Scale by Zoom
description: Compute ground metres per screen pixel for any zoom and latitude with the Map Meters per Pixel Calculator — the web map scale number. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, zoom 15 in New York is 3.619 metres per pixel — the number that tells you a screenshot's building, measured at 28 pixels, is about 100 metres long.
quick_answer: The Map Meters per Pixel Calculator computes the ground size of one screen pixel on a Web Mercator map at a zoom and latitude. Enter zoom and latitude and read the scale — the number behind screenshot measurement and every honest use of a web map as a measuring tool.
steps_intro: One pixel, priced in metres, anywhere on Earth:

body.t: Measure features in map images: pixels × m/px = ground size. The
tool multiplies it out for you.
A figure that must resolve 10 m features needs m/px well under 10 — z17 at mid-latitudes (1.19 m/px at the equator, finer poleward). Choose before you render.
Check a map's scale bar against the computed m/px — disagreement means the image was resized, a fact worth knowing before measuring anything on it.
Digital maps killed the printed scale ratio; m/px is its successor concept, and this calculator makes it tangible.
Zoom 0: 156,543 m/px (the whole world in 256 px). Each zoom halves it: z10 152.9, z15 4.77, z19 0.298. Nineteen halvings from planet to pavement.
At 60° the same zooms are worth half the metres (cos 60° = 0.5): z15 gives 2.39 m/px. Northern maps are secretly higher-resolution — Mercator's compensation for its area lies.

popular_table.title: Metres per pixel (equator)
popular_table.intro: The standard scale — multiply by cos(latitude) for elsewhere… precisely, the value at latitude = equator value × cos(lat).
popular_table.note: Based on the tile standard's equatorial circumference (2π × 6,378,137 m) over 256 × 2^zoom pixels. Screen DPI does not enter — map pixels, not device pixels.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
Ground metres per map pixel = 156,543.03392 × cos(latitude) ÷ 2^zoom — the Web Mercator scale formula, evaluated for your zoom and latitude.
Which map standard does it use?
The slippy-map standard (256-px tiles, EPSG:3857 geometry) — the scale your actual maps render at.
Can I use this in production GIS?
For display scale, yes — it is the renderer's own arithmetic. Metric analysis belongs to geodesic measurement, not pixel scale.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — the frame GPS produces and web maps consume.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — resolution is not accuracy; the precision tools on this site price each decimal place in metres.
Device pixels versus map pixels?

Retina screens pack 2 device px per map px; measurement uses map pixels — screenshots from retina displays are double-sized, and the m/px here still applies to the map's own pixel grid, so halve screenshot counts from retina captures.
North-south scale differs?
Locally in Mercator the scale is isotropic (same both directions at a point) — one number serves the point.
Printed maps?
Print scale is set by DPI and page geometry — compute from the scale bar, not from zoom logic.
Earth's equatorial circumference in the projection (40,075,016 m) divided by 256 pixels at zoom 0. The constant is geography, not convention.
fractional zooms?
Scroll zooms are fractional in modern libraries — the formula accepts them; tiles are chosen from the nearest integer level beneath.
